title: 📘 UNIT 6: ETHIOPIA — INTERNAL DEVELOPMENTS AND EXTERNAL INFLUENCES FROM 1941 TO 1991
notes:
1941 → restoration of imperial rule after Italian occupation.

1974 → Ethiopian Revolution and downfall of Emperor Haile Selassie.

1974–1991 → Derg military rule.

1991 → downfall of the Derg regime.

title: 6.1 👑 Re-establishment of Imperial Rule
notes:
1941 → Emperor Haile Selassie returned to Ethiopia after the defeat of Italy.

Major developments:
• Restoration of the imperial government.
• Centralization of state power.
• Expansion of modern administration.
• Strong relations with Britain and the USA.
• Ethiopia became increasingly involved in international organizations.

title: 6.1.1 🌍 External Influences
notes:
Post-1941 Ethiopia was influenced by the international Cold War environment.

Major external influences:

• Britain → important influence after liberation.

• USA → major military and economic partner.

• USSR → later supported revolutionary and socialist forces.

• International organizations → provided diplomatic and economic links.

📌 Ethiopia's foreign relations affected its military, economic and political development.

title: 6.1.2 🇪🇷 Eritrea and Ethiopia
notes:
1941–1952 → Eritrea was administered by Britain after Italy's defeat.

1952 → Eritrea federated with Ethiopia under a UN arrangement.

1962 → Emperor Haile Selassie abolished the federation and incorporated Eritrea into Ethiopia.

📌 Eritrean armed resistance subsequently developed into a prolonged struggle for independence.

title: 6.1.3 🏜️ The Ogaden Question
notes:
Ogaden → Somali-inhabited territory in southeastern Ethiopia.

Major issue:
• Somalia claimed parts of Ethiopia inhabited by ethnic Somalis.
• The issue became linked with Somali nationalism and irredentism.
• Ethiopia and Somalia fought over the Ogaden.

📌 The Ogaden question became a major source of conflict between Ethiopia and Somalia.

title: 6.2 🌾 Socio-Economic Conditions, 1941–1974
notes:
The imperial economy remained predominantly agricultural.

Major features:
• Agriculture was the main source of employment and income.
• Land ownership was highly unequal.
• Peasants faced various forms of taxation and obligations.
• Modern industries and infrastructure developed slowly.
• Foreign investment and trade increased.
• Education and health services expanded but remained limited.

title: 6.2.1 🌱 Agricultural Sector
notes:
Agriculture dominated the Ethiopian economy.

Major products:
• Coffee.
• Cereals.
• Oilseeds.
• Livestock.

Problems:
• Traditional farming methods.
• Low productivity.
• Land insecurity in many areas.
• Heavy taxation and rent.
• Periodic drought and famine.
• Limited agricultural technology.

title: 6.2.2 📜 Land Tenure Systems
notes:
Major land tenure systems included:

• Rist → hereditary land-use rights based on descent.

• Gult → rights to collect tribute or services from landholders.

• Gebbar → peasant system involving taxation and labor obligations.

• Private/individual ownership → increasingly important in some areas.

📌 Land tenure differed significantly between northern and southern Ethiopia.

title: 6.2.3 ⚖️ Land Reform Question
notes:
Land reform became one of the major political issues before 1974.

Major problems:
• Unequal land distribution.
• Tenant farmers paid high rents.
• Insecurity of tenure.
• Land concentration among landlords and institutions.
• Peasant dissatisfaction.

📌 The slogan "Land to the Tiller" became central to the revolutionary movement.

title: 6.2.4 🏭 Trade and Industry
notes:
Post-1941 Ethiopia experienced gradual economic modernization.

Developments:
• Growth of manufacturing.
• Expansion of roads and transport.
• Development of banking and financial institutions.
• Growth of import and export trade.
• Expansion of urban markets.
• Increasing foreign investment.

📌 Coffee became an important export commodity.

title: 6.3 ⚔️ Imperial Absolutism and Opposition
notes:
Haile Selassie's government remained highly centralized and dominated by the emperor.

Major opposition movements included:
• Peasant rebellions.
• Student movements.
• Military dissatisfaction.
• Eritrean armed struggle.
• Political and intellectual opposition.

📌 Economic inequality, authoritarian rule, land problems and political repression contributed to growing opposition.

title: 6.3.1 🌾 Peasant Rebellions
notes:
Major peasant resistance occurred in different regions because of:
• Land disputes.
• Taxation.
• Government interference.
• Religious and cultural issues.
• Landlord–tenant conflicts.

Notable examples → Gojjam, Bale and other regional rebellions.

title: 6.3.2 🎓 Student Movement
notes:
University and secondary-school students became an important source of political opposition.

Major demands:
• Land reform.
• Democracy.
• National self-determination.
• Social justice.
• End of imperial absolutism.

📌 The slogan "Land to the Tiller" became closely associated with the student movement.

title: 6.3.3 ⚔️ Eritrean Armed Struggle
notes:
After Eritrea's annexation in 1962, armed resistance intensified.

Main organization:
• Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF).
• Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) later became a major force.

📌 The Eritrean struggle became one of the major challenges facing the imperial government and later the Derg.

title: 6.3.4 🎖️ Military Mutinies and 1974 Crisis
notes:
Military dissatisfaction increased because of:
• Low salaries and poor living conditions.
• Dissatisfaction with military leadership.
• Economic crisis.
• Government weakness.
• War and internal conflicts.

1974 → military units began mutinying and demanding reforms.

📌 The crisis eventually led to the overthrow of Emperor Haile Selassie.

title: 6.4 🔥 The 1974 Ethiopian Revolution and the Derg
notes:
1974 Revolution → brought an end to the imperial regime.

Major causes:
• Land inequality.
• Political repression.
• Economic problems.
• Famine.
• Student opposition.
• Military dissatisfaction.
• Eritrean and other armed conflicts.

12 September 1974 → Emperor Haile Selassie was deposed.

Derg → military committee that took control of the state.

title: 6.4.1 🎖️ Emergence of Military Dictatorship
notes:
PMAC → Provisional Military Administrative Council, commonly called the Derg.

Major developments:
• Military government consolidated power.
• Mengistu Haile Mariam emerged as the dominant leader.
• Monarchy was abolished.
• Ethiopia was declared a socialist state.

Political groups included:
• EPRP → Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party.
• Meison → All-Ethiopian Socialist Movement.

📌 Conflict between the Derg, EPRP and Meison shaped the revolutionary period.

title: 6.4.2 🔴 Red Terror and White Terror
notes:
White Terror → urban guerrilla campaign associated mainly with EPRP attacks against the Derg and its supporters.

Red Terror → Derg campaign against suspected political opponents, especially EPRP members and supporters.

1977–1978 → Red Terror reached its most intense phase.

📌 Political violence and executions became major features of the revolutionary period.

title: 6.5 ☭ Socio-Economic and Political Measures of the Derg
notes:
Major Derg policies:
• Nationalization of land.
• Nationalization of major industries and financial institutions.
• Establishment of peasant associations.
• Establishment of urban dwellers' associations/Kebeles.
• Villagization and resettlement programs.
• Socialist economic planning.
• Centralized political control.

title: 6.5.1 🌾 Land Reform Proclamation
notes:
4 March 1975 → land reform proclamation.

Major provisions:
• Rural land became state property.
• Private ownership of rural land was abolished.
• Landlordism was abolished.
• Peasants received use rights.
• Peasant associations were established.
• Land could not be sold, mortgaged or transferred as private property.

📌 The reform aimed to end the landlord–tenant system.

title: 6.5.2 🏭 Nationalization
notes:
Major industries, banks, insurance companies and other large enterprises were nationalized.

Purpose:
• Establish state control over major economic resources.
• Reduce private capitalist ownership.
• Develop a socialist economy.
• Increase government control of production and distribution.

title: 6.5.3 🏘️ Villagization and Resettlement
notes:
Villagization → relocation of scattered rural households into organized villages.

Resettlement → movement of people from densely populated or drought-affected areas to areas considered to have greater agricultural potential.

Aims:
• Improve access to services.
• Increase agricultural production.
• Facilitate administration.
• Address drought and population pressure.

📌 Both programs were controversial and caused significant social disruption.

title: 6.5.4 ⚔️ Ogaden War, 1977–1978
notes:
1977 → Somalia invaded Ethiopia to capture the Ogaden.

Ethiopia initially faced serious military pressure.

Major change:
• USSR shifted support toward Ethiopia.
• Cuba sent troops to support Ethiopia.
• Massive military assistance reached Ethiopia.

1978 → Ethiopian forces, supported by allies, expelled Somali forces from most of the Ogaden.

📌 The war strengthened Ethiopia's alignment with the Soviet bloc.

title: 6.5.5 🏛️ Political Organization and Socialist State
notes:
The Derg gradually transformed Ethiopia into a centralized socialist state.

Major developments:
• Mass organizations were created.
• Political opposition was suppressed.
• 1984 → Workers' Party of Ethiopia established.
• 1987 → People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia established.
• Mengistu became President.

📌 Political power remained concentrated under the ruling party and military leadership.

title: 6.6 📉 Decline and Downfall of the Derg
notes:
Major internal factors:
• Prolonged civil wars.
• Eritrean independence struggle.
• Tigrayan insurgency.
• Economic problems.
• Famine and drought.
• Political repression.
• Popular dissatisfaction.

External factors:
• Declining Soviet support.
• End of the Cold War.
• Reduced military assistance.
• International pressure.
• Collapse of socialist governments in Eastern Europe.

title: 6.6.1 ⚔️ Armed Opposition
notes:
Major armed organizations included:
• EPLF → Eritrean People's Liberation Front.
• TPLF → Tigray People's Liberation Front.
• EPRDF → Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front.

📌 Armed opposition gradually weakened Derg control over the country.

title: 6.6.2 🏛️ End of the Derg Regime
notes:
1989 → EPRDF was formed as a coalition of political organizations.

1991 → Derg military control rapidly collapsed.

May 1991 → Mengistu Haile Mariam left Ethiopia.

28 May 1991 → EPRDF forces entered Addis Ababa.

📌 The Derg regime ended and a new political order began.

title: 🏆 UNIT 6 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
👑 1941 → Restoration of Haile Selassie's imperial rule.

🇪🇷 1952 → Eritrea federated with Ethiopia.

🇪🇷 1962 → Federation abolished; Eritrea annexed.

🏜️ Ogaden → major Ethiopia–Somalia territorial dispute.

🌾 Imperial land system → rist + gult + gebbar + tenancy.

🎓 Student movement → land reform + democracy + social justice.

🔥 1974 → Ethiopian Revolution.

12 September 1974 → Haile Selassie deposed.

🎖️ Derg/PMAC → military government.

🔴 Red Terror → Derg campaign against political opponents.

⚪ White Terror → EPRP's urban armed campaign.

🌾 4 March 1975 → Land Reform Proclamation.

🏭 Nationalization → major industries, banks and insurance companies.

⚔️ Ogaden War → 1977–1978 → Ethiopia defeated Somali forces with major Soviet/Cuban support.

🇪🇹 1987 → People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.
